subject: english-language-and-literature
title: English Language and Literature MYP 5 eAssessment Paper A (3 tasks, 80 marks)

questions.content:
[[Q 1.1 | A 2]]
Task 1: Analysing
Questions 1.1 to 1.4 focus on the key concept of perspective. Question 1.5 focuses on the key concept of connections.  The criteria assessed are A (Analysing) and B (Organizing). Suggested time for Questions 1.1 to 1.4: 15 minutes. Suggested time for Question 1.5: 35 minutes.

Text A: 'Declaration' (a poem, written for this paper)
This poem is spoken by a young woman at an airport border desk.

Nothing to declare, I say,
and the officer's pen hovers
over the little box marked Purpose of Visit.
 
What I carry: one suitcase, zipped like a held breath;
a jar of my mother's pickled lemons,
sealed with wax, sweating in the heat of my hand;
a name that the machine pronounces
as three separate mistakes.
 
Nothing to declare.
But my grandmother's language
is rattling in my throat like loose change,
and I am afraid that if I open my mouth
it will spill across the counter,
and they will count it, and find it
not legal tender here.
 
Stamp.
The sound is small and final,
a door closing in a distant house.
 
Welcome, he says.
I say Thank you in his accent.
It fits like a borrowed coat.
Outside, rain.
I lift the jar to my face
and breathe my whole country in.

Text B: social media post and replies (written for this paper; in the live exam this would be an on-screen image)
[Visual: a square photograph shows a cluttered kitchen table. On it are a steaming pot, three mismatched bowls, and a hand-written card reading 'Welcome Table - every Sunday - bring nothing, bring anyone'. Warm yellow light, shot from above. A hand reaches in from the edge of the frame holding a ladle.]

@thewelcometable (Nour A.)
"Two years ago I arrived in this city knowing nobody. Nobody asked me my story, they just asked if I was hungry. 🍲 So now it's my turn. Every Sunday, my flat, soup for whoever needs it. No forms. No questions. Just a seat. #WelcomeTable #SundaySoup #NewNeighbours"

♥ 2,431 likes · 318 shares

Replies:
@marcus_k: "Crying at my desk. Sat alone for a year. See you Sunday."
@old_mrs_hale: "I will bring a lemon cake. Is that allowed?"
@nour.a replied to @old_mrs_hale: "Everything is allowed. That's the whole point."
@dan_t_1987: "Nice idea but where does it end? Who pays for all this soup?"
@nour.a replied to @dan_t_1987: "Nobody counts a pot of soup. Come and see for yourself."

Q 1.1 Comment on the use of the word 'declare' and the title of Text A. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 2 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies the idea of declaring or customs without explanation, e.g. the title refers to an airport. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): comments on the title or repeated phrase with some explanation, e.g. 'Nothing to declare' repeats like a refrain; officially she has nothing to declare, but the poem shows she carries language, memory and identity that cannot be declared on a form. [1] Award 0 for no or incorrect reference to the text.

questions.content:
[[Q 1.2 | A 3]]
Refer to Text A (printed in Question 1.1). Explain the effect of the simile 'a name that the machine pronounces / as three separate mistakes'. Include a second image from stanza two in your answer. (3 marks)

Note: the simile is in stanza two; the second image may be any other figurative expression in that stanza.
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 3 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies a figure of speech without developing the effect, e.g. the machine gets her name wrong. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes an effect with some explanation, e.g. the mispronounced name suggests technology and the new country fail to recognise her identity. [1] Level 3 (3 marks): explains the effect consistently with well-chosen quotation, e.g. 'three separate mistakes' turns her name from something whole into errors, so the speaker feels she is the problem; the image of the language 'rattling in my throat like loose change' links her heritage to something small and worthless in the new place, adding to the sense of shame. [1] Accept 'zipped like a held breath' as the second image.

questions.content:
[[Q 1.3 | A 2]]
Refer to Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Describe the purpose of the hashtags and the hand-written card in the post. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 2 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies a purpose without explanation, e.g. the hashtags help people find the post. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes a purpose with an example, e.g. the hashtags #WelcomeTable and #NewNeighbours make a recognisable brand and let like-minded people find and share the event, while the card 'bring nothing, bring anyone' reads as personal and informal, inviting trust. [1]

questions.content:
[[Q 1.4 | A 3]]
Refer to Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Analyse the effect of the replies from @dan_t_1987 and @nour.a. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 3 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies an effect with no development, e.g. one person disagrees. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes the effect of the exchange with some justification, e.g. the sceptical question gives a realistic opposing voice, making the project look tested. [1] Level 3 (3 marks): analyses the effect consistently with precise reference, e.g. the question 'where does it end? Who pays?' voices economic worry, and Nour's short reply 'Nobody counts a pot of soup' answers calmly with a metaphor of generosity, then invites the sceptic ('Come and see for yourself') rather than arguing, which reinforces her inclusive tone and persuades readers to trust her. [1]

questions.content:
[[Q 1.5 | A 10 | B 10]]
Refer to Text A and Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Compare and contrast how the two texts explore what it means to arrive in a new place. (Approximately 350 words) (20 marks)

Criterion A (Analysing) is worth 10 marks and Criterion B (Organizing) is worth 10 marks.
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A (10 marks) and Criterion B (10 marks), 20 marks in total. Criterion A (10 marks): 9 to 10 marks for effective, perceptive analysis of content, language, structure and technique in both texts with extensive, well-chosen evidence; 6 to 8 for considerable analysis with sufficient, relevant evidence; 3 to 5 for adequate analysis with some evidence; 1 to 2 for limited analysis with few or no examples. Indicative content: Text A uses first-person free verse, a refrain ('Nothing to declare'), extended contrast between official language and private feeling, sensory imagery (pickled lemons, wax, rain), simile ('like a borrowed coat', 'like loose change') and a final turn of private comfort ('breathe my whole country in'). The tone moves from anxiety to quiet resilience and the poem stays internal and solitary. Text B uses multimodal features: overhead warm-lit photograph, the hand with a ladle (offering), informal direct address, emoji, imperative short sentences ('No forms. No questions. Just a seat'), hashtags and the dialogue of replies. Arrival is shown as community and welcome after earlier isolation. Contrast: loss of identity and fear of rejection versus rebuilding belonging by giving hospitality; private reflection versus public persuasion; both use food as a symbol of home and connection (lemons, soup). Award up to [10] for Criterion A. Criterion B (10 marks): 9 to 10 marks for effective organisation: clear structure, comparison and contrast sustained throughout, effective linking and a conclusion; 6 to 8 for a considerable degree of organisation with sustained comparison; 3 to 5 for an adequate degree of organisation with some comparison; 1 to 2 for limited organisation, with the texts mostly treated separately. Indicative content: a clear introduction naming both texts; a sustained point-by-point or thematic structure; comparative connectives; paragraphs that each pair evidence from both texts; a conclusion that evaluates the shared use of food and the contrasting emotional outcome. Award up to [10] for Criterion B.

questions.content:
[[Q 2.1 | C 10 | D 10]]
Task 2: Producing literary text
This task focuses on the key concept of creativity. The criteria assessed are C (Producing text) and D (Using language).

Image 1 (described in words): a night-time view from inside a train carriage. A window is misted over and someone has drawn a small house in the condensation with one finger. Beyond the glass, blurred orange lights stream past. A child's backpack sits on the seat, with one strap trailing on the floor.
Image 2 (described in words): an empty classroom at dusk. Every chair is stacked on its desk except one, which stands alone in the middle of the room facing the whiteboard. On the board, half-rubbed-out, is the single word 'Tomorrow'.

Using one of the images, write the opening of a story set in a dystopian society in which a young character notices something the authorities want hidden. You may consider purpose, characterisation, setting, mood and point of view. State which image you are using before you start. (Approximately 350 words) (20 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion C (10 marks): 9 to 10 marks for a high degree of insight and imagination, perceptive stylistic choices and extensive precise detail; 6 to 8 for considerable insight and imagination, thoughtful choices and sufficient detail; 3 to 5 for some insight and imagination, some stylistic choices and some detail; 1 to 2 for limited insight, few stylistic choices and little detail. Indicative content: a named image used meaningfully; a controlled dystopian setting built through telling detail (rules, surveillance, scarcity) rather than explanation; a developed character and viewpoint; a hook or revelation; atmosphere created through imagery, sentence length and pacing. A response that uses neither image nor the prompt scores 0 for C. Award up to [10] for Criterion C. Criterion D (10 marks): 9 to 10 marks for an effective range of vocabulary and sentence structures, consistently suitable register and high accuracy with only minor errors; 6 to 8 for a varied range, considerable accuracy and errors that do not hinder communication; 3 to 5 for an adequate range, a degree of accuracy and errors that sometimes hinder communication; 1 to 2 for a limited range, with errors that often hinder communication. Indicative content: precise, varied vocabulary, deliberate sentence variety (short sentences for tension, longer for description), figurative language, consistent tense and point of view, accurate punctuation of dialogue if used. Award up to [10] for Criterion D.

questions.content:
[[Q 3.1 | B 10 | C 10 | D 10]]
Task 3: Producing non-literary text
This task focuses on the key concept of communication. You will create a piece of non-literary writing in relation to the global context identities and relationships: identities, and personal, physical, social and cultural expression. The criteria assessed are B (Organizing), C (Producing text) and D (Using language).

You have recently moved to a new country with your family. Write an informal letter to a friend in your old home town describing the first month, what you miss, and how your sense of who you are has changed. (Approximately 350 words) (30 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion B (10 marks): organisation suited to an informal letter: address or date, greeting, clear paragraphs sequencing first impressions, losses and change, and a warm sign-off; 9 to 10 effective, 6 to 8 considerable, 3 to 5 adequate, 1 to 2 limited. Award up to [10] for Criterion B. Criterion C (10 marks): perspective on identity shown through insight, personal detail and examples (language, food, school, friendships); 9 to 10 high degree of insight and extensive detail, 6 to 8 considerable, 3 to 5 some, 1 to 2 limited. Award up to [10] for Criterion C. Criterion D (10 marks): conversational register with control, varied sentences, humour or emotion, rhetorical questions or direct address to the friend, accurate grammar and punctuation; 9 to 10 high accuracy and effective register, 6 to 8 considerable, 3 to 5 a degree, 1 to 2 minimal. Award up to [10] for Criterion D.
